messages:
jordan: Hey team — we have a customer reporting intermittent 429s and huge tail latency when they do short interactive chats. Happens mostly during bursts (many users opening sessions at once). They say it feels like throttling even though their token usage is within quota. Can someone sanity-check?

alex: Thanks Jordan. Do we have the request ids / sample logs? 429s normally mean rate limit/quota or the per-minute burst policy.

jordan: I asked for logs. They sent this snippet from their client logs: 
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
X-Request-Id: req_01F8Z...a9
X-RateLimit-Limit: 600
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 167
{"error":{"message":"rate limit exceeded"}}
```
Plus their app-level traces show lots of short requests with a rotating session_id per chat tab.

sara: Two quick hypotheses: 1) they’re hitting a token or request-per-minute quota on the API key (hosted). 2) continuous batching + KV cache mismatch is increasing effective qps because many cache misses create extra model work per message.

michael: Can you explain the continuous batching / KV cache angle?

sara: Sure — if client opens many independent sessions without stable session identifiers, the server can’t reuse KV cache (prefixes) between turns. That means every turn is a full forward rather than an efficient incremental decode. With continuous batching, lots of tiny full requests get batched together into big batched model calls — which increases token work and can trigger per-project burst limits. It looks like throttling to the customer because latency spikes and some requests 429.

alex: Also worth checking how the client is hinting for batching. If they set a fresh conversation_id per interaction, their cache miss rate will be high. A repro is helpful. Jordan — did they share an example request body?

jordan: Yes, here's a sanitized curl they used to repro: 
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood-inference.com/v1/generate \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-xxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"rwkv-7b","input":"hi","session_id":"tab-352-164","use_kv_cache":true,"batch_hint":{"max_batch_size":32,"max_latency_ms":100}}'
```
They open ~300 tabs quickly in a stress test.

michael: That makes sense — high cardinality session_id + high max_batch_size. When those many parallel short requests arrive, scheduler forms large batches which temporarily saturate model capacity and also increase per-request latency (queueing). If quota is measured in model token-equivalents or in concurrent model calls, this explains the 429.

support-bot: Note: customer is on Hosted tier with default per-key burst policy of 600 r/min. If they want sustained higher throughput, recommend Dedicated or increase quota.

alex: Actionable steps to troubleshoot and mitigate (sorted):
1) Ask customer to run a small repro that keeps session_id stable across turns for a single user and compare. Stable session_id should lower cache misses and CPU/GPU work.
2) Ask them to lower client batch_hint parameters: set max_batch_size=8 and max_latency_ms=40 to reduce giant batch formation.
3) Check token-level metrics in Redwood Console: token rate, model invocations, cache hit/miss (if enabled) for their API key and time window around 429s.
4) Collect server-side request ids for a sample 429 and provide to support; include request headers and X-Request-Id.
5) As a short-term app-side change, implement exponential backoff with jitter on 429 and 503.

jordan: I relayed steps. They ran two quick experiments: A) keep same session_id per user — tail latency dropped ~60% and 429s stopped. B) kept rotating session ids but set max_batch_size=6 and max_latency_ms=25 — fewer 429s but slightly higher p50 latency.

sara: Perfect — that aligns with expectations. For the record, recommend they use session affinity keys for KV caching (session_id or conversation_id) so prefix KV cache works. Also enable prefix cache TTL on their route (we can check if they already have caching enabled).

michael: For deeper investigation we can pull traces for req_01F8Z...a9 and neighbors. Jordan — please ask for timestamps (they already gave 1793401200-ish) and a sample request id for both a successful request and a 429. We'll attach traces.

jordan: Will do. Also they asked whether continuous batching is 'throttling' them intentionally. How do we phrase this?

alex: Short answer: Not intentionally. Continuous batching tries to maximize throughput by grouping small requests. That can cause higher instantaneous demand (bigger model invocations) which may hit quotas or saturate the runtime, producing 429s or increased latency. So it's an emergent behavior from batching + many cache misses, not an access-denial heuristic.

sara: Additional config knobs to suggest: 
- use per-route `grouping_key` set to conversation_id so scheduler batches similar sessions together, improving KV cache locality.
- enable partial prefix caching (store the last N tokens per session) to reduce recompute on short turns.
- lower `max_batch_delay_ms` to reduce queueing latency during spikes.
- if they need consistent low latency at scale, recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity.

ops-bot: FYI — current infra shows a small spike in queued batches in region us-west-2 at 1793401100-1793401400, consistent with this customer's repro window. No infra errors.

michael: Good to note. Jordan — if they want more throughput, they can either: 1) stabilize session ids and tune batching, or 2) request a temporary quota bump (we can escalate to product infra) or 3) move to Dedicated.

jordan: One more thing — they saw inconsistent cache behavior: sometimes cache hit rate is high even with rotating session ids. Could that be because of request coalescing?

sara: Yes — if two requests arrive with identical input prefix within the batching window, the runtime can coalesce and reuse KV state for that batch, causing apparent hit. But it's not reliable if session ids differ. Coalescing depends on input prefix equality, not session id.

alex: I'll draft a short response for the customer with reproducible steps, the quick config changes, and the ask for request ids + console screenshots. Jordan — can you paste the final message you plan to send?

jordan: Draft below — feel free to edit: 
"Hi — thanks for the repro steps. We reproduced the behavior. Root cause appears to be a combination of high-cardinality session ids (leading to KV cache misses) plus large continuous batching parameters. This increases model work per unit time and hit your burst limits, causing 429s. Please try: 1) keep session_id stable per conversation; 2) set max_batch_size=8 and max_latency_ms=40; 3) implement exponential backoff on 429/503; 4) send us the request ids for a failed and a succeeding call and screenshots of your token usage in the Console. If you need sustained higher throughput, we can discuss a Dedicated plan or temporary quota increase."

sara: Nice. Add an optional troubleshooting curl for them to test stable session: 
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood-inference.com/v1/generate \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-xxxx' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"rwkv-7b","input":"hey again","session_id":"user-123","use_kv_cache":true}'
```
And note to include the X-Request-Id header value from responses.

michael: I'll pull the trace once Jordan posts the request ids. If we confirm runtime saturation we can propose a quota adjustment.

jordan: Thanks all, sending reply now. Closing loop after we get request ids. :thumbsup:
